# Abstract

The classical epoch of South Asia, spanning from the accession of Chandragupta I in 319AD to the rise of regional mediaeval kingdoms around 750AD, represents a transformative phase in the subcontinent's demographic and agrarian history. Across a vast territory of 3,94M km² (encompassing 3.938.787 km² and 51.246 active terrestrial grid cells), human settlement integrated the imperial heartlands of the middle and lower Ganga with the fertile alluvial deltas of Bengal and Assam, the semi-arid maritime littoral of Gujarat and Saurashtra, the river valleys of the Indus and Punjab, and the volcanic black-cotton plateaux of the Vakataka Deccan. Far from witnessing systemic demographic retrenchment, the era was defined by expansive rural colonisation, royal copper-plate land grants (*shasanas* and *agrahara* endowments), sophisticated hydraulic engineering and resilient agrarian communities that accommodated fluctuating monsoonal regimes.

Under the INDUS regional reconstruction, macro-regional population grew from 52M inhabitants in 319AD to 56,5M in 400AD, climbing to 59M in 500AD at the height of Imperial Gupta hegemony. Following sixth-century Huna disruptions, the fragmentation of central authority and the subsequent political consolidation under Harsha of Kannauj (606AD to 647AD) and contemporary regional dynasties (Maitrakas of Valabhi, Gauda rulers, Kamarupa kings and Later Guptas), population advanced steadily to 61M in 600AD, 62,5M in 650AD and reached 64M by 750AD. Aggregate population density increased from 13,2 persons per km² in 319AD to 16,25 persons per km² in 750AD.

Demographic mass remained anchored in the Gangetic plain and eastern riverine deltas. By 750AD, the Madhyadesha and Magadha core (21,76M inhabitants, 34% of subcontinental total) and the Gauda, Bengal and Kamarupa macro-province (14,08M, 22%) concentrated more than 55% of all inhabitants on just 27,76% of the land area. The Madhyadesha core achieved the highest provincial density at 47,06 persons per km², sustained by perennial Himalayan snow-melt tributaries, intensive double-cropping of rice and wheat, and ancient urban hubs such as Varanasi, Patna, Kannauj and Mathura. In contrast, the extensive western and north-western provinces of Malwa and Gujarat (12,8M, 13,13 persons per km²), Punjab, Kashmir and Sindh (8,32M, 7,61 persons per km²), and the Vakataka Deccan (7,04M, 9,06 persons per km²) sustained lower aggregate densities, though punctuated by prominent commercial emporia and royal citadels including Ujjain, Valabhi, Bharuch, Multan, Peshawar, Lahore and Kanchipuram.

This study reconstructs the historical demography of classical South Asia by coupling 3.183 georeferenced settlement trajectories with comprehensive epigraphic inventories of copper-plate land grants, archaeological surveys of habitation mounds, palaeoclimatic speleothem records and classical travelogues, notably those of Faxian and Xuanzang. By evaluating settlement subtraction against archaeological reality, the reconstruction demonstrates that urban transformation during the mid-first millennium AD represented functional decentralisation and rural agrarian intensification rather than continental demographic collapse.

# Political Architecture and Regional Sub-Divisions

## Imperial Guptas and the Madhyadesha Core

The political landscape of northern and central South Asia was reshaped during the fourth century AD by the rise of the Imperial Gupta dynasty from its ancestral base in eastern Uttar Pradesh and Magadha [@neill2020empires; @mishra2026historical]. Chandragupta I (c. 319AD to 335AD) established imperial sovereignty, forming an alliance with the Lichchhavis and assuming the title of *Maharajadhiraja*. His successor, Samudragupta (c. 335AD to 375AD), recorded his extensive military campaigns on the famous Prayaga stone pillar inscription composed by his court poet Harishena. The inscription delineates a multi-tiered imperial structure: direct annexation of the rulers of Aryavarta in the Gangetic basin, subjugation and tributary subordination of forest kingdoms (*atavika rajyas*) in central India, and tributary recognition from frontier potentates in Kamarupa, Samatata, Kartripura and Nepal [@neill2020empires; @dwivedi2021tools].

Chandragupta II Vikramaditya (c. 375AD to 415AD) extended Gupta authority to the Arabian Sea by subjugating the Western Kshatrapas (Sakas) in Malwa and Saurashtra, securing control over lucrative maritime trade conduits operating through Bharuch, Cambay and Sopara [@seland2014archaeolog; @sheikh2004state]. Dynastic matrimonial alliances cemented this vast sphere: Prabhavatigupta, daughter of Chandragupta II, married Rudrasena II of the Deccan Vakataka dynasty, eventually ruling as regent over Vidarbha and coordinating northern and southern political spheres [@neill2020empires; @policardi2024goddess]. Under Kumaragupta I (c. 415AD to 455AD), the founding of Nalanda Mahavihara marked the pinnacle of state patronage for higher learning and monastic organisation [@shaw2013archaeolog; @verardi2018gods].

By the late fifth century AD, incursions by the Alkhan Hunas under Toramana and Mihirakula fractured imperial control in the north-west and Punjab [@morris2019central; @verardi2012buddhism]. Skandagupta (c. 455AD to 467AD) mounted successful defensive campaigns, recorded in the Bhitari pillar inscription and the Junagadh rock inscription commemorating the repair of the Sudarshana lake embankment [@singh2020hydrology]. Nevertheless, succession disputes, economic realignments and the rise of ambitious feudatories (*samantas*) led to political devolution. In the sixth and seventh centuries, regional powers emerged: the Maitrakas of Valabhi in Saurashtra, the Pushyabhutis of Thanesar and Kannauj under Prabhakaravardhana and Harsha, the Later Guptas of Magadha and Malwa, Shashanka of Gauda in Bengal, and the Varman dynasty in Kamarupa [@targa1999pala; @kovacs2024bengal; @sharma2011empire].

## Territorial Organisation and Administrative Hierarchy

Imperial governance across classical South Asia operated through an articulated hierarchical administrative geography that balanced centralised royal oversight with corporate local self-governance [@neill2020empires; @mishra2026historical]. At the apex of provincial administration stood the province, designated as a *desha*, *rashtra* or *bhukti*, governed by a royal prince (*kumaramatya*) or an imperial viceroy titled *uparika* or *uparikamahadanda-nayaka* [@neill2020empires]. Prominent examples include Pundravardhana bhukti in North Bengal, Tirabhukti in North Bihar, and Saurashtra rashtra in western India.

Each *bhukti* was partitioned into administrative districts termed *vishayas*, supervised by a district magistrate (*vishayapati*) whose headquarters (*adhishthana*) coordinated regional tax collection, judicial administration and police defense [@kovacs2024bengal; @dwivedi2021tools]. The *vishayas* were subdivided into sub-districts known as *vithis*, which comprised clusters of agricultural villages termed *gramas*. At the village level, administration was conducted by the headman (*gramika*) or village elders (*mahattaras*), collaborating with the local council (*panchamandali*) to maintain boundary records, settle property disputes and apportion shared obligations for maintaining irrigation canals, tanks and protective embankments [@singh2020hydrology; @targa1999pala].

The coordination between royal officials and local agrarian leaders ensured that tax obligations (*bhaga*, *kara* and *bali*) were assessed according to seasonal crop yields rather than arbitrary quotas. Village assemblies preserved records of land ownership, irrigation rights and communal pastures on cloth or palm-leaf scrolls (*pustakas*), which were verified by village accountants (*pustapalas*) before any property transfer could be inscribed on copper plates [@neill2020empires; @dwivedi2021tools].

## Numismatic Evidence and Currency Spheres

Numismatic discoveries provide critical insights into imperial fiscal capacity, trade connections and metallic standards across the classical era [@dwivedi2021tools; @neill2020empires]. The Imperial Guptas minted magnificent series of gold coins (*dinaras*), initially struck on the Kushan weight standard of approximately 120 to 123 grains (7,8 to 8 grams) and later reformed by Skandagupta to the national Indian *suvarna* standard of 144 grains (9,3 grams) [@dwivedi2021tools]. Obverse types, including the Archer, Lion-Slayer, Tiger-Slayer, Horseman and Asvamedha types, celebrated imperial paramountcy and martial prowess, while the reverse consistently featured the goddess Lakshmi or Ganga [@policardi2024goddess].

Following the annexation of western India by Chandragupta II, the empire introduced silver currency modelled directly on the drachms of the Western Kshatrapas [@sheikh2004state]. These silver issues, weighing approximately 30 to 34 grains, met the monetary requirements of western commercial trade across Gujarat and Malwa. Copper coinages were issued in limited quantities, primarily in the Malwa and Mathura sectors [@khattak2025major]. For everyday market transactions, low-value agricultural exchanges and rural bazaar commerce, cowrie shells (*kapardaka*) functioned as the primary currency, as explicitly observed by Faxian during his fifth-century travels through Madhyadesha [@dwivedi2021tools]. The persistence of cowries, gold dinaras and silver drammas demonstrates that monetisation remained adapted to distinct commercial tiers rather than suffering sudden demonetisation.

## Five Macro-Provinces

INDUS partitions classical South Asia into five physiographically and politically coherent macro-provinces bounded by mountain ranges, major river divides and climatic boundaries (Table \ref{tab:subregions}):

### Madhyadesha, Magadha and Prayaga-Kannauj Core

The Madhyadesha and Magadha core (462.384 km², 11,74% of the regional domain) forms the imperial axis of northern India, spanning the fertile doabs between the Yamuna and Ganga rivers eastward into the Magadhan plain of southern Bihar. Encompassing celebrated classical cities including Pataliputra (Patna), Varanasi, Kanyakubja (Kannauj), Mathura, Kaushambi, Ayodhya, Shravasti and Rajgir, this province sustained the densest rural population in the subcontinent [@hawkes2020back; @khattak2025major]. By 319AD, its population stood at 17,68M (38,24 persons per km²), rising to 19,21M in 400AD, 20,06M in 500AD and reaching 21,76M by 750AD (47,06 persons per km²). The province concentrated 34% of the entire macro-regional population on less than one-eighth of its land.

Beyond its agrarian primacy, the province functioned as the ideological and ritual nucleus of the empire. The sacred confluence of the Ganga and Yamuna at Prayaga served as the setting for royal redistributive assemblies, culminating in the quinquennial assemblies convened by Harsha where royal treasuries were systematically distributed to religious figures, scholars and the indigent [@targa1999pala; @verardi2018gods].

### Gauda, Pundravardhana, Samatata and Kamarupa

Spanning Bengal and the Brahmaputra valley of Assam (631.135 km², 16,02%), this province encompasses the humid lower deltas of the Ganga, Brahmaputra and Meghna river systems [@kovacs2024bengal; @sharma2011empire]. Supported by abundant rainfall, perennial inundation and deltaic sedimentation, agricultural colonisation expanded rapidly across active deltaic tracts. Epigraphic records document extensive land grants across Pundravardhana (North Bengal), Vanga (Southern Bengal), Samatata (Eastern Bengal delta) and Kamarupa [@targa1999pala]. Major regional centres included Gaur (Lakshmanavati), Mahasthangarh (Pundranagara), Tamralipti, Chandraketugarh, Karnasuvarna and Pragjyotishpura (Guwahati). Population expanded from 11,44M in 319AD to 12,98M in 500AD and reached 14,08M by 750AD (22,31 persons per km²).

### Malwa, Ujjain, Maitraka Valabhi and Western Provinces

Covering 975.022 km² (24,75% of regional area), this expansive western province encompasses the fertile black-cotton Malwa plateau, the Vindhyan scarplands, the Gulf of Khambhat and the semi-arid peninsulas of Gujarat and Saurashtra [@sheikh2004state; @kumar2025investigat]. Ujjain served as a primary political and astronomical hub, while Valabhi functioned as the capital of the Maitraka dynasty and an internationally renowned centre of Buddhist scholarship [@verardi2018gods]. Ports such as Bharuch (Bhrigukachchha), Cambay and Patan connected overland caravan routes with Indian Ocean maritime networks [@seland2014archaeolog; @cobb2018black]. The provincial population rose from 10,4M in 319AD to 11,8M in 500AD and reached 12,8M by 750AD (13,13 persons per km²).

### Punjab, Thanesar, Kashmir and North-Western Frontier

The north-western province (1.093.083 km², 27,75%) encompasses the five rivers of the Punjab basin, the Vale of Kashmir, the Potohar plateau, the middle and lower Indus valley of Sindh, and the frontier corridors linking South Asia with Central Asia [@petrie2017adaptation; @morris2019central; @verardi2012buddhism]. Thanesar (Sthanvishvara) served as the ancestral base of the Pushyabhuti dynasty before Harsha transferred his capital to Kannauj. Other prominent centres included Taxila, Peshawar (Purushapura), Multan, Lahore, Sialkot (Sakala) and Mansura. Population climbed from 6,76M in 319AD to 7,67M in 500AD and reached 8,32M by 750AD (7,61 persons per km²), reflecting lower agricultural carrying capacities in arid interfluvial tracts balanced by intensive irrigated cultivation along river inundation belts [@green2019discoverin; @garciamolsosa2023reconstruc].

### Vakataka Vidarbha and Northern Deccan Sphere

The southern macro-province (777.163 km², 19,73%) covers the northern Deccan plateau, primarily modern Vidarbha, Khandesh and northern Maharashtra, extending into the northern fringes of the Krishna-Godavari doab [@shaw2013archaeolog; @neill2020empires]. Governed by the Vakatakas from capitals at Nandivardhana and Pravarapura, the region witnessed brilliant artistic and architectural patronal activity, epitomised by the rock-cut Buddhist chaityas and viharas at Ajanta during the reign of Harishena (c. 475AD to 500AD) [@shaw2013archaeolog]. Coastal and peninsular trading hubs including Sopara, Kalliena and Kanchipuram linked the Deccan with maritime routes [@seland2014archaeolog]. Provincial population increased from 5,72M in 319AD to 6,49M in 500AD and reached 7,04M by 750AD (9,06 persons per km²).

# Agrarian Expansion, Water Management and Land Grants

## Epigraphic Charters and Agrarian Colonisation

A central dynamic of the classical period was the systematic expansion of the agrarian frontier facilitated by royal land grants inscribed on copper plates (*tamra-shasana*) and stone stelae [@neill2020empires; @targa1999pala]. Rulers of the Gupta, Vakataka, Maitraka, Gauda and Kamarupa lineages granted uncultivated tracts (*khila*), forest margins (*aranya*) and entire revenue-bearing villages (*grama*) to learned Brahmins (*brahmadeya*), religious institutions (*devagrahara*) and Buddhist viharas [@shaw2013archaeolog; @dwivedi2021tools].

These charters conferred extensive fiscal immunities: exemption from regular royal taxes (*kara*, *bhaga* and *bhoga*), immunity from the entry of royal soldiers and revenue collectors (*a-chata-bhata-praveshya*), and rights to mineral, timber and water resources. In return, grant recipients served as agrarian pioneers, organising forest clearance, introducing calendar-based agricultural techniques and integrating indigenous tribal populations into caste-based agrarian structures [@neill2020empires; @kovacs2024bengal]. In Bengal, copper plates from Damodarpur, Baigram and Gunaighar document the purchase of fallow state land by private individuals for donation to religious establishments, revealing an active land market and community involvement in rural boundary demarcation [@kovacs2024bengal].

## Epigraphic Corpus and Territorial Demarcation

The epigraphic record of land transactions reveals a highly formalised administrative mechanism for agrarian registration and boundary demarcation across northern India [@neill2020empires; @targa1999pala]. In northern Bengal (Pundravardhana bhukti), the five famous Damodarpur copper plates, dating from the reigns of Kumaragupta I and Budhagupta, detail the operation of the district administrative board (*adhikarana*) headed by the district officer (*ayuktaka*) alongside the chief merchant (*nagara-shreshthin*), caravan leader (*sarthavaha*), chief artisan (*prathama-kulika*) and chief scribe (*prathama-kayastha*) [@kovacs2024bengal]. Private buyers petitioned the board to purchase uncultivated fallow land (*aprahata-khila*) at the customary rate of three dinaras per *kulyavapa* (a land measure based on seed sown) to endow religious institutions.

Similarly, the Baigram copper plate of 448AD records the purchase of state land by two Brahmin brothers for the maintenance of a temple of Govindasvamin, with village record-keepers (*pustapalas*) conducting physical boundary surveys before royal confirmation [@kovacs2024bengal]. The Gunaighar copper plate of Vainyagupta (507AD) in Samatata grants land to the Mahayana Buddhist Vaivartika Sangha, specifying precise boundary markers including river distributaries, marsh edges and drainage channels. In Vidarbha, the Poona copper plate of Prabhavatigupta and the Rithpur plates of the Vakataka queen Bhavattarika document the donation of entire agricultural villages in the Wardha valley, establishing institutional religious networks that anchored rural cultivation in the Deccan [@shaw2013archaeolog; @neill2020empires].

## Hydraulic Engineering, Tank Irrigation and Water Lifting

Sustaining high demographic densities required advanced hydraulic infrastructure to mitigate seasonal precipitation deficits [@singh2020hydrology; @shaw2003ancient]. Ancient Indian texts, including the *Brihat Samhita* of Varahamihira and the *Arthashastra* tradition, dedicate substantial treatises to water prospecting, reservoir siting and dam construction [@singh2020hydrology].

Archaeological excavations confirm the widespread construction of irrigation tanks (*tataka*), storage reservoirs (*vapi*) and stepped masonry wells across central and western India [@shaw2003ancient]. In Vidisha and Sanchi, Shaw and Sutcliffe documented an extensive network of ancient earthen dams and irrigation reservoirs dating to the early historic and classical periods, engineered to capture monsoon runoff from sandstone plateaux and release water through masonry sluices into surrounding agricultural plains [@shaw2003ancient]. In Saurashtra, the Junagadh inscription of Skandagupta records the breach of the monumental Sudarshana lake embankment during severe storms in 456AD and its restoration within two years by the provincial governor Parnadatta and his son Chakrapalita, who constructed a masonry dam one hundred cubits wide and forty cubits high [@singh2020hydrology].

Technological innovations in water lifting expanded irrigation beyond riverbanks. The *arahatta* or pot-garland wheel (*ghati-yantra*), rotated by bullock or manual labour, enabled continuous extraction of groundwater from deep masonry wells, permitting the cultivation of dry-season crops such as barley, wheat and sugarcane across northern India and Gujarat [@singh2020hydrology; @dwivedi2021tools].

## Monsoon Dynamics and Agrarian Resilience

High-resolution speleothem palaeoclimate records from Sahiya Cave and regional lake sediment cores indicate that the mid-first millennium AD experienced fluctuating Indian Summer Monsoon (ISM) precipitation [@dixit2014abrupt; @rakesh2022ecological]. A stable and relatively humid climatic interval characterised the fourth and fifth centuries AD, supporting agricultural expansion across the northern river valleys [@jha2025geoarchaeo]. Towards the mid-sixth century AD, palaeoclimatic proxies record intervals of monsoon weakening, contemporaneous with global climate cooling linked to volcanic sulphate veils in 536AD and 540AD [@dixit2014abrupt; @islam2020late].

The diversification of cropping systems provided vital resilience against environmental volatility [@petrie2017adaptation; @singh2017counter]. Agrarian communities practiced multi-cropping regimes: deep-water winter rice (*aman*) and autumn rice (*aus*) in the humid Bengal delta, paired with *kharif* summer millets and *rabi* winter pulses, wheat and oilseeds across the drier western plains [@petrie2017adaptation; @kovacs2024bengal]. The extensive distribution of irrigation tanks and groundwater wells buffered crop production against delayed monsoon rains, preventing localized droughts from degenerating into regional famines.

## Agro-Ecological Zonation and Cropping Regimes

The diverse ecological zones of classical South Asia sustained highly specialised agricultural regimes matched to local soil and rainfall conditions [@singh2020hydrology; @petrie2017adaptation; @rakesh2022ecological]. In the lower Gangetic delta and coastal Bengal, the primary staple was deep-water transplanted winter rice (*shali*), supplemented by broadcast autumn rice (*vrihi*) and spring rice (*boro*) along river depressions [@kovacs2024bengal]. Classical agronomic treatises such as the *Krishi-Parashara* and the *Brihat Samhita* describe careful seed selection, organic manuring using cow dung and oilseed cake, and astrological calendar management for synchronising sowing with the onset of the *Rohini* and *Ardra* nakshatras [@singh2020hydrology].

Across the drier western and north-western doabs of Uttar Pradesh, Punjab and Sindh, agriculture was anchored in a dual-cropping cycle (*kharif* and *rabi*) [@petrie2017adaptation; @singh2017counter]. Summer monsoon crops included pearl millet (*bajra*), sorghum (*jowar*), sesamum (*tila*) and cotton (*karpasa*), while winter cultivation produced wheat (*godhuma*), barley (*yava*), chickpeas (*chanaka*), mustard (*sarshapa*) and lentils (*masura*). In Malwa and Gujarat, the moisture-retentive black-cotton soils (*regur*) supported extensive cotton and sugarcane (*ikshu*) plantations, providing high-value agricultural cash commodities that fueled textile manufacturing and long-distance caravan trade [@sheikh2004state; @dwivedi2021tools].

# Settlement Hierarchies and the Urban-Decline Debate

## Archaeology of Classical Urban Centres

Classical South Asia maintained an intricate settlement hierarchy ranging from imperial metropolises and provincial administrative capitals to fortified market towns (*nigama*), trading ports (*pattana*) and nucleated agrarian villages [@bettencourt2021introducti; @hawken2021long]. Archaeological mound surveys and remote sensing across northern and north-western India have identified thousands of settlement mounds (*tepe* or *theri*) displaying continuous occupational strata from the early historic through classical periods [@orengo2020automated; @green2019discoverin; @garciamolsosa2023reconstruc; @petrie2025hidden].

In Madhyadesha, major urban centres were characterised by monumental burnt-brick architecture, paved drainage conduits, domestic brick wells and extensive terracotta manufacturing [@khan2013bricks; @hawkes2020back]. Pataliputra (Patna), though losing its exclusive status as primary imperial capital, remained an expansive political and commercial centre, concentrating 141.687 inhabitants at its peak in 500AD. Varanasi maintained comparable demographic mass (141.687 peak), functioning as an unexcelled pilgrimage, weaving and craft manufacturing centre [@hawkes2020back].

Kannauj (Kanyakubja) experienced dramatic demographic expansion as it evolved from a regional Gupta provincial headquarters into the imperial capital of the Maukhari and Pushyabhuti realms. Its population climbed from 45.769 in 400AD to 59.615 in 500AD and peaked at 66.538 in 600AD. When the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang visited Kannauj in 636AD during Harsha's reign, he recorded a magnificent metropolis four miles long and one mile wide, enclosed by formidable defensive moats and high towers, housing one hundred Buddhist monasteries and more than two hundred Deva temples [@targa1999pala; @verardi2018gods].

In the north-west, Delhi (Indraprastha) anchored critical overland routes between the Gangetic divide and Punjab, supporting 170.025 inhabitants at its fifth-century peak. Lahore (113.350 peak), Multan (66.121 peak) and Peshawar (61.398 peak) served as primary emporia along trans-Indus trade arteries [@khattak2025major; @morris2019central]. In western India, Ujjain (61.398 peak) integrated overland routes from the Gangetic valley with the coastal ports of Gujarat, while Valabhi (30.000 peak) functioned as the bustling political and educational capital of the Maitrakas [@sheikh2004state; @verardi2018gods].

## Structural Evolution of Excavated Gangetic Cities

Systematic excavations across the Gangetic basin illuminate the material reality of urban transformations between the fourth and eighth centuries AD [@hawkes2020back; @khan2013bricks]. At Ahichchhatra in Bareilly district, extensive stratigraphy demonstrates the construction of massive tiered brick temples (notably Temple AC II) dedicated to Shiva, alongside magnificent terracotta sculptures depicting the river goddesses Ganga and Yamuna dating to the Gupta period [@hawkes2020back]. Although residential density within the fortified enclosure reorganised in the post-Gupta era, religious monumentalism and surrounding settlement mounds persisted through the eighth century AD.

At Kaushambi, excavations around the Ghoshitarama monastery and royal palace complex demonstrate substantial structural rebuilding under the Guptas, followed by evidence of destruction attributed to the Hunas under Toramana [@hawkes2020back; @morris2019central]. Nevertheless, occupation continued across peripheral mounds. At Rajghat (ancient Varanasi), excavations revealed continuous structural phases characterised by fired-brick dwellings, public drainage systems, sealings and terracotta figurines spanning the entire first millennium AD without systemic occupational hiatus [@hawkes2020back]. In Bengal, excavations at Rajbadidanga in Murshidabad district confirmed the identification of Karnasuvarna, the seventh-century capital of Shashanka, revealing extensive monastic and residential foundations that flourished alongside deltaic agrarian colonisation [@kovacs2024bengal; @targa1999pala].

## Re-evaluating Urban Decay and Ruralisation

A prominent historiographical debate has centred on the degree of urban vitality during the post-Gupta era. Historians associated with the Indian feudalism thesis posited a widespread urban decay (*shahar hras*) between 300AD and 1000AD, arguing that the decline of long-distance Roman commerce, coin shortages and the proliferation of land grants led to de-urbanisation, economic self-sufficiency and the ruralisation of society [@dwivedi2021tools; @seland2014archaeolog].

Recent archaeological syntheses and field surveys challenge this monolithic model [@hawkes2020back; @garciamolsosa2023reconstruc; @petrie2025hidden]. While certain early historic cities in the middle Gangetic valley (such as Kaushambi, Shravasti and Rajgir) experienced physical contraction or structural reorganisation in their core monumental zones, this process was accompanied by the simultaneous emergence and expansion of new regional urban nodes [@hawkes2020back; @bettencourt2021introducti]. Settlement shifted towards regional political centres like Kannauj, Valabhi, Karnasuvarna and Gaur, as well as rural market centres and temple complexes that stimulated local exchange networks [@targa1999pala; @kovacs2024bengal]. Far from demonstrating aggregate demographic decline, the archaeological record demonstrates a redistribution of urban populations across a more decentralized, polycentric regional network [@hawken2021long; @bettencourt2021introducti].

Epigraphic records from western and central India further demonstrate the vitality of inter-regional merchants and itinerant traders (*sarthavahas*) during the post-Gupta centuries [@dwivedi2021tools; @sheikh2004state]. Inscriptions from Gwalior, Kota and Kaman record gifts by merchant corporations and oil-millers to local sanctuaries, confirming that capital accumulation continued outside imperial capitals [@neill2020empires]. Moreover, the continuity of craft specialization across early mediaeval temple towns indicates that urbanization in South Asia followed a polycentric evolutionary trajectory rather than a unilinear boom-and-bust cycle [@hawkes2020back; @bettencourt2021introducti]. As regional administrative seats took root in Bengal, Gujarat and the Deccan, commercial exchange reorganized around local agricultural hinterlands, ensuring resilient economic integration across changing political regimes [@targa1999pala; @kovacs2024bengal].

## Monastic Complexes and Knowledge Networks

Buddhist Mahaviharas and Brahmanical temple complexes played a structural role in regional demographic and economic organization [@shaw2013archaeolog; @verardi2018gods; @morris2021economic]. Monasteries were not isolated ascetic retreats, but major landholders, consumers of agricultural surplus and centres of manufacturing and literacy. Nalanda, established in the fifth century AD under Kumaragupta I, expanded into a sprawling monastic university that housed several thousand resident scholar-monks, supported by revenues from more than two hundred endowed villages [@shaw2013archaeolog; @verardi2018gods].

Monastic establishments in Saurashtra, notably at Valabhi, received extensive endowments from Maitraka rulers, serving as centres of intellectual exchange and international pilgrimage frequented by Chinese scholars such as Yijing [@sheikh2004state; @verardi2018gods]. In eastern India, monastic centres at Paharpur (Somapura) and Mainamati (Salban Vihara) anchored rural colonization in the Bengal delta, functioning as nodes of literacy, legal administration and technological dissemination [@targa1999pala; @kovacs2024bengal].

## Guild Organisations and Artisan Production

A defining feature of classical urban economies was the institutional organisation of craftspeople and merchants into autonomous guilds (*shreni*, *nigama* and *puga*) [@dwivedi2021tools; @neill2020empires]. Epigraphic records and clay sealings discovered at Bhita, Basarh (ancient Vaishali), Rajghat and Nalanda attest to corporate bodies of oil-millers (*tailika-shreni*), potters (*kumbhakara*), weavers (*tantuvaya*), metalworkers and ivory-carvers operating under their own customary laws (*shreni-dharma*) recognized by imperial courts [@hawkes2020back; @khattak2025major].

These guilds performed sophisticated commercial and banking functions, receiving perpetual cash endowments (*akshaya-nivi*) from royals and wealthy citizens, paying regular interest to fund daily lamps in temples or food for Buddhist monks [@shaw2013archaeolog; @verardi2018gods]. The celebrated fifth-century Mandasor stone inscription of Kumaragupta I and Bandhuvarman records that a guild of silk-weavers (*pattavaya*) migrated from Lata (southern Gujarat) to Dashapura (Mandasor in western Malwa), attracted by the enlightened patronage of the local ruler, and pooled their collective resources to construct and later renovate a magnificent sun temple [@sheikh2004state; @dwivedi2021tools]. Such collective civic agency proves that urban artisan communities remained active and resilient corporate institutions throughout the classical period.

## Maritime Commerce and Trade Corridors

Although western trade with the Roman Empire evolved following the crisis of the third century AD, maritime connectivity in the Indian Ocean remained robust [@seland2014archaeolog; @cobb2018black]. Sasanian Persia and the Byzantine Empire maintained active commercial exchanges with western Indian ports. Ports along the Gulf of Khambhat and Saurashtra, including Bharuch (37.783 peak), Cambay and Sopara (14.169 peak), exported cotton textiles, indigo, fine ceramics, iron and semi-precious stones to Persian Gulf and Red Sea destinations [@seland2014archaeolog; @dwivedi2021tools].

In the Bay of Bengal, maritime routes expanded dramatically between eastern India and Southeast Asia. Tamralipti (23.615 peak) in the Ganges delta served as the premier international port for maritime voyages to Sri Lanka, Java, Sumatra and China [@kovacs2024bengal]. Chinese pilgrims Faxian (in 411AD) and Xuanzang (in 637AD) both embarked from Tamralipti on their homeward voyages. The circulation of cowrie shells as everyday currency alongside gold dinaras and silver drammas facilitated both local village transactions and international maritime trade [@dwivedi2021tools; @sheikh2004state].

The *Christian Topography* of Cosmas Indicopleustes, composed around 550AD, confirms that ports such as Kalyan, Chaul and Bharuch handled heavy maritime freight, exchanging pepper, silk and aromatics between South Asia, Ceylon, Sasanian Persia and the Mediterranean [@seland2014archaeolog; @cobb2018black]. Furthermore, coastal communities constructed stone-anchored jetties and beacon installations along the Kathiawar peninsula to facilitate navigation across seasonal cyclone tracks [@sheikh2004state; @kumar2025investigat].

# Methodological Framework and Spatial Calibration

## Spatial Engine and Environmental Covariates

To distribute population across the 3.938.787 km² domain, the INDUS spatial engine models 51.246 active 5-arcminute terrestrial cells. Each grid cell is evaluated using biophysical and accessibility covariates:
- Fluvial distance decay: proximity to major perennial river channels (Ganga, Yamuna, Brahmaputra, Indus, Narmada, Tapti, Godavari and Krishna), applying exponential density attenuation beyond 25 km from navigable waterways.
- Topographic wetness and terrain slope: penalising steep Himalayan and Western Ghat scarps while favouring flat alluvial terraces and fertile volcanic plateaux.
- Monsoon precipitation and agricultural suitability: incorporating regional rainfall isohyets, soil water storage capacity and multi-cropping potential [@singh2020hydrology; @petrie2017adaptation].
- Archaeological mound and site density: incorporating surveyed site clusters identified through remote sensing and historical survey records [@orengo2020automated; @green2019discoverin; @petrie2025hidden].

## Settlement Subtraction and Rural Allocation

To isolate nucleated urban populations from rural agriculturalists, 3.183 catalogued settlements with chronological population series are georeferenced to their exact WGS84 coordinates. At each benchmark year, the active population of catalogued settlements within each macro-province is aggregated and subtracted from the provincial demographic envelope.

The residual rural population is then allocated across non-settled pixels in proportion to the calibrated environmental suitability index. A two-pass boundary smoothing filter ensures continuous demographic gradients across provincial frontiers, preventing artificial density cliffs along administrative borders.

## Uncertainty Envelopes and Demographic Bounds

Every provincial and regional benchmark estimate incorporates an explicit symmetric uncertainty bound (+/- 23% across all benchmark years from 319AD to 750AD). In 500AD, the macro-regional total of 59M is bounded between 45,43M and 72,57M inhabitants. This uncertainty envelope accommodates historical variance in household size multipliers, urban density assumptions and epigraphic land measurement interpretations.

## Chronological Demographic Trajectories

### Early Gupta Rise and Consolidation (319AD to 400AD)

Between the founding of the Gupta era in 319AD and the closing years of Chandragupta II's reign around 400AD, the subcontinent experienced steady demographic expansion under unified imperial administration [@neill2020empires]. Regional population grew from 52M in 319AD to 56,5M in 400AD (+8,65%), reflecting an annual growth rate of 0,1%.

During this phase, political stability eliminated internal transit tariffs across northern India, stimulating artisan production and inter-regional grain transport [@dwivedi2021tools]. The Madhyadesha core expanded from 17,68M to 19,21M inhabitants, while Gauda and Bengal rose from 11,44M to 12,43M. When the Chinese pilgrim Faxian travelled across northern India between 399AD and 412AD, he described Madhyadesha as a prosperous, peaceful country where the people were numerous and happy, free from oppressive corporal punishments or transit registries [@hawkes2020back].

### Classical Zenith and Imperial Apex (400AD to 500AD)

The fifth century AD represented the imperial zenith of classical Indian civilization [@neill2020empires; @shaw2013archaeolog]. Regional population advanced from 56,5M in 400AD to 59M in 500AD (+4,42%), achieving an aggregate density of 14,98 persons per km².

Under Kumaragupta I and Skandagupta, state resources supported monumental architecture, irrigation maintenance and academic institutions. Agricultural colonisation extended into the forested tracts of central India and the deltaic islands of Bengal [@kovacs2024bengal]. Major urban settlements reached their historical population peaks during this interval: Patna and Varanasi both supported 141.687 inhabitants, Delhi reached 170.025, Lahore reached 113.350, and Ujjain concentrated 61.398 people.

### Huna Incursions and Regional Fragmentation (500AD to 600AD)

The sixth century AD brought major geopolitical transformations. Incursions by the Hunas fractured imperial authority in Punjab and the north-west, sacking cities such as Taxila and disrupting trans-Eurasian trade routes [@morris2019central; @verardi2012buddhism]. In the imperial core, succession disputes weakened the Later Guptas, while regional feudatories declared independence.

Despite political decentralization, demographic momentum continued, driven by expanding rural agriculture and local land grants [@targa1999pala]. Regional population grew from 59M in 500AD to 61M in 600AD (+3,39%). Growth shifted towards emerging regional capitals: Kannauj grew from 59.615 to 66.538, while Valabhi expanded from 23.077 to 30.000 as Maitraka rulers established autonomous commercial jurisdiction across Gujarat [@sheikh2004state].

### Harsha of Kannauj and the Post-Gupta Re-alignment (600AD to 650AD)

The first half of the seventh century AD was dominated by Harshavardhana of Kannauj (606AD to 647AD), who reunited northern India from Punjab to the borders of Bengal and the Narmada [@targa1999pala; @verardi2018gods]. Harsha established Kannauj as the premier metropolis of northern India, documented in detail by Banabhatta in the *Harshacharita* and by Xuanzang in his *Si-Yu-Ki*.

Subcontinental population expanded from 61M in 600AD to 62,5M in 650AD (+2,46%). Xuanzang travelled extensively throughout the subcontinent, describing teeming rural populations, flourishing orchards and fertile grain fields, alongside flourishing monastic establishments in Nalanda, Valabhi and Kanchipuram [@shaw2013archaeolog; @verardi2018gods].

### Pre-Mediaeval Equilibrium (650AD to 750AD)

Following Harsha's death in 647AD, northern India entered an era of tri-partite regional competition involving the Later Guptas of Magadha, the rising Gurjara-Pratiharas of Rajasthan, the Rashtrakutas of the Deccan and the Palas of Bengal [@targa1999pala; @kovacs2024bengal]. Regional population reached 64M by 750AD (+2,4% over 650AD), yielding an aggregate density of 16,25 persons per km².

In eastern India, the foundation of the Pala dynasty under Gopala around 750AD brought stability to Bengal, establishing Gaur (Lakshmanavati) as a premier regional capital supporting 120.000 inhabitants. In Gujarat, Patan (Anhilwara) emerged as a major commercial city supporting 50.000 people. The decentralised agrarian economy established during the Gupta era matured into the regional kingdoms of the early mediaeval period.

The urban hierarchy of classical South Asia was topped by Delhi (Indraprastha) in the north-western borderlands, which concentrated 170.025 inhabitants at its fifth-century peak [@khattak2025major]. In the Madhyadesha core, twin imperial metropolises at Patna (Pataliputra) and Varanasi maintained peak populations of 141.687 inhabitants in 500AD, retaining 98.077 inhabitants in 750AD [@hawkes2020back]. Gaur in the Bengal delta expanded dramatically to 120.000 inhabitants by 750AD under early Pala patronage [@kovacs2024bengal; @targa1999pala]. Lahore (113.350 peak) and Multan (66.121 peak) anchored the agrarian and commercial corridors of Punjab and the lower Indus valley [@morris2019central; @petrie2017adaptation].

Kannauj (Kanyakubja) achieved its peak of 66.538 inhabitants around 600AD, maintaining 59.615 in 650AD under Harsha and 45.769 in 750AD [@targa1999pala]. Ujjain (61.398 peak) and Peshawar (61.398 peak) served as pivotal junction points linking overland and maritime commerce [@sheikh2004state; @khattak2025major]. In the southern Deccan sphere, Kanchipuram reached 56.675 inhabitants in 500AD, serving as a celebrated Pallava royal capital and educational centre [@shaw2013archaeolog; @seland2014archaeolog]. Patan (50.000 in 750AD), Taxila (48.356 peak) and Mathura (47.229 peak) anchored specialized regional manufacturing, pilgrimage and scholastic activities [@khan2013bricks; @verardi2012buddhism].

By coupling georeferenced settlement trajectories with comprehensive spatial kriging and environmental suitability covariates, INDUS accounts for nucleated urban centers while allocating rural agricultural populations across the non-settled landscape, establishing a quantitative baseline for classical South Asian demography.
